en.content:
Hong Kong is still absorbing the shock of the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po, and today’s focus rightly turns from the tragedy itself to questions of governance and responsibility. A former member of the estate owners’ board says relevant government agencies “failed in their duties” despite having received complaints about a renovation project. Whether every detail will be proven in subsequent processes is for the authorities and investigators to determine, but the underlying message is unmistakable: when warnings surface early, the public expects effective, timely enforcement rather than reassurance after damage is done.

At the same time, it would be simplistic to treat this as only a story of blame without considering how complex building management can be. Renovation works involve multiple parties—owners, contractors, technical assessment, supervision arrangements—each step requiring clarity over standards, reporting, and follow-up. In a dense city like Hong Kong, the burden on regulatory systems is heavy, and information can be fragmented. Yet complexity cannot be an excuse for inaction. The real yardstick should be whether complaints trigger the right inspection depth, whether risk is escalated according to established mechanisms, and whether corrective measures are actually completed and verified.

Public trust is not built through statements after incidents; it is built through demonstrable responsiveness. For future cases, residents will want clearer communication channels for complaint handling, more transparent timelines for inspections and remedial orders, and stronger accountability when reviews conclude that problems exist—or when they fail to prevent them. This is not about adversarial politics; it is about protecting lives and ensuring that the city’s “safety net” functions as a net, not as a post-event record.

As Wang Fuk Court residents begin returning to salvage belongings, the emotional weight should not be overshadowed by procedural debates. But neither should official review be confined to condolence. If enforcement gaps are indeed established, the community will expect concrete improvements—upgraded supervision standards, tightened oversight of renovation compliance, and clearer roles across departments. Only then can the public reasonably believe that lessons learned translate into action, and that prevention receives the same urgency as response.

zh.content:
今日本港最值得正視嘅新聞，係大埔王福邨翻新工程疑雲中，政府相關部門「未能履行職責」嘅指控。事件已經唔單止係一單工程管理或監察失誤，而係牽涉到公營房屋安全、監管問責、同居民當初投訴點樣被接收、跟進同處理。當一位屋苑業主立案架構嘅前成員，喺聆訊上直指執法與監管失職，社會要問嘅就唔係「當時有冇做過啲咩」，而係「做嘅有冇對準真正風險」、流程有冇足夠力度去阻止悲劇發生。

與其用單一事件去搵替罪羊，更應拆解成整套制度問題：投訴由邊個受理、如何分級、多久跟進、專業判斷有冇被量化成可執行標準、同埋一旦出現警號，政府係以「行政合理」定係以「風險可接受」做決策。若居民早已提出擔憂，監管部門卻未能把警示轉化為即時介入或嚴格檢查，咁責任就唔只係個別官員疏忽，而係「制度產生失效」——亦即問責鏈條喺關鍵時間點斷咗。

不過，社評亦應承認一點：在高密度公共屋邨、翻新工程高度複雜嘅現實下，任何監管都可能遇到資訊不足、技術不確定或協調困難。真正考驗唔係有冇風險，而係政府面對風險時，係唔係採取保守、前置、防止災害嘅做法——例如更透明嘅投訴追蹤機制、更可核查嘅執法紀錄、同埋對關鍵時點嘅獨立覆核。只要制度能夠證明自己「即使資料未完備，都會先保安全再補細節」，公眾先至會信服。

我嘅立場係：今次聆訊唔可以止於「指出失職」，而要逼使政府提出可驗證、可量化嘅改善方案，包括明確交代投訴由接收到行動嘅時間表、增強跨部門協同嘅責任分工、以及建立讓居民得以查核嘅跟進報告。安全唔應該靠運氣，亦唔應該由事後補救去彌補制度空隙。當監管失效被公開指控，社會最應該守住嘅底線，就係確保公共資源同監察機制，真係能夠在危險萌芽時就攔停。
